title: June minutes reveal opposite year-end rate paths beneath a unanimous hold
summary: All twelve voters at the 16–17 June meeting supported a 3.50–3.75% federal funds target. The minutes published on 8 July reveal the limits of that unanimity. A few participants thought the evidence already supported a hike yet agreed to wait. In their individual most likely scenarios for year-end, many placed the appropriate rate inside or slightly below the current range. Many others placed it above. The disagreement persisted even when participants restricted themselves to what they personally regarded as the likeliest economic outcome. A market reading that translated twelve votes to hold into an expectation of twelve votes for steady rates in December would overlook the most important policy information in the discussion.

The Committee changed the way it communicated that uncertainty. A majority saw advantages in shortening the postmeeting statement. Most participants wanted to drop language they thought suggested an easing bias. Members approved a statement retaining the commitment to ample reserves and explicitly promising to restore price stability; the chair described plans for five independent task forces on monetary policy. The removal of an easing preference made it easier to convey genuinely two-sided scenarios. It did not make a rate increase the new majority baseline. Several participants thought the rate was already insufficiently restrictive or provided no restraint, while a few others judged it slightly restrictive. That differing starting point helps explain why similar economic observations could support different paths.

In the staff's economic review, annual PCE inflation stood at 3.8% in April and core PCE at 3.3%. Using consumer and producer price data, staff estimated May headline inflation at 4.1% and core at 3.4%. Housing services inflation had eased, but firmer nonhousing services inflation roughly offset it. Staff attributed the pickup in goods prices to past tariff increases and pressure in technology markets, as well as the effects of the Middle East conflict on energy and other inputs. A sharp increase in petrol prices could subsequently reverse and pull headline inflation down without securing much improvement in core inflation. Indeed that was the shape of the staff forecast for the second half of 2026. Staff lifted the current- and following-year projections relative to April and expected inflation near 2% in 2028. This was an assessment conditional on the forecast assumptions, distinct from the Committee's own objective and from participants' individual projections.

AI investment mattered both for the size of demand and the timing of capacity. Participants heard spending plans that continued to exceed earlier expectations. Data centres and other projects needed equipment and electricity immediately, while gains in productivity from adopting the technology might arrive later. Staff saw real private domestic final purchases growing faster than GDP in the second quarter. Investment in technology, software and equipment helped account for that strength. Strong imports as well as exports of high-tech goods linked the US expansion to Asian producers. At the same time, weaker confidence and higher energy costs weighed on activity in Europe and in lower-income Asian economies. A single global growth assumption would miss these offsetting effects on US import demand, foreign sales and commodity costs.

The debate was about whether demand associated with the buildout would run above capacity long enough to affect prices across the economy. Most participants saw that as a route to more persistent inflation. They also heard from businesses reluctant to raise prices lest they lose customers. Those firms could absorb some pressure in margins in the short term. Other participants expected disinflation in housing services and eventual productivity gains. Wages offered limited support for a broad overheating diagnosis. May unemployment was 4.3%. The private-sector employment cost index rose 3.4% in the year to March, and hourly earnings also rose 3.4% in the year to May, half a percentage point less than a year earlier. Many participants judged pay trends compatible with the inflation goal. A declining job-finding rate nevertheless left some concerned about how well the market would withstand a shock.

The distribution of spending power reinforced that distinction. High equity valuations, earnings and tax refunds supported consumption, particularly for higher-income households. Participants also reported that poorer households were relying more on credit and facing greater pressure from petrol and grocery prices. Staff described credit as readily available to larger firms and municipalities but tighter for small businesses and borrowers with lower scores. Public corporate and leveraged-loan issuance remained strong while private credit issuance had slowed. Business development companies were seeing slower inflows and more requests for redemptions. A broad equity rally and firm aggregate consumption could therefore coexist with restraint for borrowers most sensitive to current debt service.

The Desk review explains why even a marked increase in Treasury yields could not be read as a simple signal about inflation. A US–Iran memorandum and hopes for less disruption lowered oil futures and near-term inflation compensation relative to April. The ten-year Treasury yield nevertheless rose about 20 basis points after the April meeting and about 50 basis points from the beginning of the conflict. Staff attributed much of the rise in nominal rates over the intermeeting period to higher real rates, particularly at shorter maturities. The manager also noted a gradual shift in Treasury ownership from relatively price-insensitive public-sector investors to more price-sensitive private holders, with possible implications for term premia. The dollar appreciated as short-term US rates rose relative to those in other advanced economies. Equities climbed nearly 6% on the S&P 500, led by technology and stronger earnings expectations despite the increase in yields.

Both traded prices and Desk respondents broadly anticipated a June hold. At longer horizons the median survey respondent's most likely path had no move through early 2027 and a cut in its second quarter, whereas market pricing embedded a hike by mid-2027. The manager judged that part of the difference could be compensation for bearing rate risk. A mode, an expected value and a traded forward rate need not agree. The policy discussion adds a second explanation consistent with the evidence: participants saw materially different year-end outcomes as plausible. Neither the survey distribution nor the minutes supply a probability to assign to each Committee scenario.

The operating evidence shows how short-term rates can move independently of the selected policy range. In mid-May repo rates fell to 15 basis points below interest on reserve balances; the effective funds rate declined two basis points. The manager cited several possible contributors. Reserves recovered from the April tax-date low as Treasury's account declined. Reserve-management purchases increased reserves and reduced bills available to private investors. Dealer intermediation, leveraged investors' financing demand and seasonal cash investment by housing agencies also changed. Modest reverse-repo use on especially soft days supported the floor. The manager continued to assess reserves as ample; the Board retained interest on reserve balances at 3.65%. A two-basis-point market move is consequently neither a policy cut nor sufficient evidence of an intentional easing in financial conditions.

The public-information sequence matters. The June rate, the shorter statement and the participants' economic projections were already available after the meeting. The July release elucidated the disagreement over neutral and restrictive settings and the scenarios in which some of the same people would accept either easing or tightening. The nearly 6% equity gain and the 20-basis-point rise in the ten-year yield belong to the Desk's account of the period preceding the June meeting. They cannot measure the response to those additional details in July.

questions.question: Did AI capital spending raise demand faster than it expanded productive capacity?
questions.detail: Compare orders, equipment and power prices, construction activity, completed capacity and output per hour in exposed industries. Separate the date a facility is financed from the date it begins producing. Broad price pressure and margin changes after allowing for energy and tariffs would carry more weight than an isolated relative-price increase in a scarce input.

questions.question: Why did surveyed policy paths and traded forward rates point in different directions for mid-2027?
questions.detail: Align observation dates, compare like horizons and distinguish each respondent's mode from their probability-weighted mean. Use options to examine the sizes of both tails and real-yield estimates to test sensitivity to term premia. The minutes provide candidate explanations for the divergence but do not identify a unique probability distribution.

questions.question: Was repo softness an adjustment within an ample-reserves system or evidence of a lasting change in rate control?
questions.detail: Compare repo and unsecured funding rates with administered rates around Treasury cash flows, bill supply changes and reserve purchases. Examine facility usage, dealer financing demand and whether rates normalised as seasonal cash demand receded. The mid-May low is an informative episode only if its timing can be distinguished from these overlapping influences.

questions.question: Did the 8 July release materially alter beliefs about the balance of risks?
questions.detail: Compare rate futures and options immediately before and after publication with what the June statement, projections and later public remarks had already revealed. Trace any repricing to the expected path, upside tail or downside tail. Even a stable mean could conceal a change in the distribution investors thought consistent with the Committee's reaction function.
